lede: Ask where something is, not how far it has gone. Pick a point on the line, call it zero, and this graph tracks the position from that point, second by second.
can: Read a position, sign included, off a displacement/time graph.
Find a velocity as the gradient of one stage, using that stage's own time.
Draw the graph of a journey told in words, joint by joint.

md: A distance/time graph only ever climbs, because distance keeps adding up. A displacement/time graph can come back down: its height is a live position, how far the body is from the chosen point, with a minus sign for the far side of it. Read a height and you have read where the body was at that moment.

stem: Use the robot's graph to find its displacement from the pharmacy door when $t = 10$ s and when $t = 55$ s.

steps.decision: Go up from 10 to the first section and across to the axis. The section climbs 30 m in 20 s, so half way along it is at 15 m.
Up from 55 meets the falling section below the time axis: the robot is 6 m past the door, on the far side.

prompt: The robot's graph is flat at 30 m from 20 s to 35 s. What is its displacement when $t = 30$ s, in metres?
explain: The height of the graph is where the robot is. Straight up from 30 s meets the flat section, and across from there is 30 m, as in step 1 of See it: the robot is parked 30 m from the door.

twin.prompt: The robot's graph falls in a straight line from 30 m at $t = 35$ s to $-15$ m at $t = 60$ s. What is its displacement when $t = 45$ s, in metres?
twin.explain: It falls 45 m in 25 s, 1.8 m each second, so 10 s after the start of that section it is at $30 - 18 = 12$ m.

caption: A stage's rise over its own run is its velocity.

md: A straight section changes the displacement by the same amount every second, and that amount is the velocity. Take the two joints of the section: the rise is the finishing displacement minus the starting one, the run is the finishing time minus the section's own starting time. Rise over run, sign kept.

The size of the gradient is the speed and its sign is the direction: a steeper section means a faster body, whichever way it slopes, and a section sloping down means the body is moving back towards the start.

stem: Find the velocity of the robot during the last section of its journey.

steps.decision: Write the two ends of the section as coordinates before anything else.
Finish minus start, both ways. The run is the time this section lasted, not the clock reading 60.
The minus sign is the direction: the robot is heading back towards the door.

title: GCSE Mechanics Further - Displacement Time
why: A Northern Ireland teacher working from the CCEA Unit 2 specification: watch each section treated on its own before anything is added up.

prompt: Work out the velocity of the robot during the first 20 seconds, in m/s.
explain: The first section runs from $(0, 0)$ to $(20, 30)$: rise 30 m over its own run of 20 s, so $30 \div 20 = 1.5$ m/s, away from the door. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it on the first section.

twin.prompt: A straight section of a displacement/time graph runs from $(5, 12)$ to $(13, 44)$, with displacement in metres and time in seconds. What is the velocity, in m/s?
twin.explain: Rise $44 - 12 = 32$ m over a run of $13 - 5 = 8$ s: $32 \div 8 = 4$ m/s.

md: Flat means the displacement is not changing, so the body has stopped: somewhere, not necessarily at the start. A falling straight section means the displacement is shrinking, so the body is heading back, at a steady negative velocity.

title: Why falling is not slowing
md: A straight section, however steep, has one gradient all the way along it, so the velocity does not change there. A line sloping down is a body going the other way at a steady rate, not a body slowing down.

stem: Describe the three stages of the trolley's journey shown on its displacement/time graph.

steps.decision: Climbing straight: moving away from the start at a steady 4 m/s.
At rest for 8 s, 24 m from the start, not back at it.
Falling straight: a steady velocity back past the start, finishing 12 m beyond it. Nothing is slowing.

prompt: The robot's last section falls in a straight line from 30 m to $-15$ m. What is the robot doing?
options: Travelling back past the pharmacy door at a steady velocity
Slowing down and stopping at the pharmacy door
answer: Travelling back past the pharmacy door at a steady velocity
explain: A straight falling section is one steady negative velocity: the body is coming back, and here it goes on below zero, past the door. This is step 3 of See it, where the trolley did the same.

twin.prompt: A straight section of a displacement/time graph falls from 10 m to $-5$ m. What is the body doing?
options: Moving back past its start at a steady velocity
Slowing down to a stop at its start
twin.answer: Moving back past its start at a steady velocity
twin.explain: Straight means steady; falling means heading back; ending below zero means past the start.

optionNotes.option: Slowing down to a stop at its start
optionNotes.why: Straight means steady: nothing is slowing, and it does not stop at the start, it passes it.
The height of the graph is a position along the line, not a height above the ground.

optionNotes.option: Slowing down and stopping at the pharmacy door
optionNotes.why: A falling line looks like something winding down, but a straight section has one steady velocity; it is heading back, not slowing.
The graph is not a picture of the corridor: its height is the distance from the door, not a height above the ground.

md: Distance counts every metre covered, whichever way the body was going, so it only grows. Displacement is one signed reading at the end. For the distance take each sloping section, find the size of its change and add the sizes; for the displacement read one number off the axis.

stem: The graph shows a courier robot's displacement from a lift door. Find the total distance it travels and its displacement at the end.

steps.decision: The first sloping section climbs 25 m.
It falls from 25 m to $-35$ m: 25 m down to the axis and 35 m more. The size of the change is the distance for that leg.
Add the sizes; the flat section adds nothing.
One reading off the axis: 35 m on the far side of the door.

prompt: A displacement/time graph rises from 0 m to 18 m, stays level, then falls in a straight line to −9 m. What total distance does the body travel, in metres?
explain: Each leg counts as a length: 18 m out, then from 18 m down to $-9$ m, which is 27 m. So $18 + 27 = 45$ m. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it. The $-9$ is where it ends, its displacement, not a distance.

twin.prompt: A displacement/time graph rises from 0 m to 14 m, stays level, then falls in a straight line to −6 m. What total distance does the body travel, in metres?
twin.explain: 14 m out and 20 m back, from 14 m to $-6$ m: $14 + 20 = 34$ m.

alt: A displacement/time graph with two straight lines: P, solid, from (0, 0) to (50, 300), and Q, dashed, from (0, 330) to (50, 80). They cross.

caption: Two bodies on one line: where their graphs cross, they are at the same place.

md: Two bodies can share one set of axes, each line read exactly as before. Where the lines cross, the displacements are equal: the two bodies are at the same point, passing each other. Read the time off the bottom and the position off the side, and check it from the two velocities. Lines sloping opposite ways mean the bodies are moving towards each other.

stem: P and Q move along the same straight track. When do they pass each other, and where?

steps.decision: Read straight down from the crossing to the time axis.

steps.working: P: velocity $300 \div 50 = 6$ m/s, so at $30$ s it is at $6 \times 30 = 180$ m
steps.decision: Check the reading from P's own gradient.

steps.working: Q: velocity $\dfrac{80 - 330}{50} = -5$ m/s, so at $30$ s it is at $330 - 5 \times 30 = 180$ m
steps.decision: Q starts 330 m out and comes back. The same 180 m: they pass there.

prompt: On one displacement/time graph, A's line runs from (0, 0) to (40, 200) and B's from (0, 180) to (40, 20). At what time do they pass each other, in seconds?
explain: A moves at $200 \div 40 = 5$ m/s and B at $\dfrac{20 - 180}{40} = -4$ m/s. They meet when $5t = 180 - 4t$, so $9t = 180$ and $t = 20$ s. This is steps 2 and 3 of See it: each position from its own velocity.

twin.prompt: On one displacement/time graph, A's line runs from (0, 0) to (30, 210) and B's from (0, 195) to (30, 15). At what time do they pass each other, in seconds?
twin.explain: A moves at 7 m/s and B at $-6$ m/s: $7t = 195 - 6t$, so $13t = 195$ and $t = 15$ s.

md: **From words to a graph** (Summer 2024). The journey is told along a line through lettered points, and you draw it. Write each joint as a coordinate first; the last joint is wherever the words leave the body, not on the time axis.

**A rate from your own graph** (Summer 2024). The next part asks for an average speed or a velocity from what you drew. Take lengths from your joints; a velocity is one stage's own rise over its own run.
**Below the axis** (CCEA Teacher Guidance). A displacement can be negative: the body is past its start, on the far side. The graph carries on below the time axis; it does not stop at it.
**Two journeys, one grid** (Teacher Guidance; Summer 2023 and 2026 set two journeys on velocity/time graphs). Where two displacement lines cross, the bodies are at the same point.

stem: A trolley leaves O and travels 45 m along a straight track to A in 10 s. It waits at A for 6 s, then travels 60 m back along the track in 15 s. Draw its displacement/time graph.

figure.alt: The trolley's displacement/time graph: from (0, 0) up to (10, 45), level to (16, 45), then down to (31, −15), below the time axis.

steps.decision: Start at O, then 45 m out after 10 s: write each joint as a coordinate first.
Waiting keeps the displacement at 45 m for 6 s. Two sections are now fixed.
60 m back from 45 m ends at $45 - 60 = -15$ m, below the axis, at $16 + 15 = 31$ s.

steps.working: Three straight lines, stopping at $t = 31$ s
steps.decision: Join the joints and stop: nothing is drawn after the journey ends.

prompt: You have drawn a displacement/time graph but cannot see how to get the velocity of one stage. What is worth writing first?
options: The coordinates of the two ends of that stage
The total distance for the whole journey
answer: The coordinates of the two ends of that stage
explain: A velocity is one stage's rise over its own run, and the two joints of that stage, written as coordinates, put both subtractions in front of you. That is what step 1 of See it does before anything else.

optionNotes.option: The total distance for the whole journey
optionNotes.why: It feels like progress, but a velocity belongs to one stage and needs that stage's own change and own time, not the whole trip.
An average covers the whole journey; the velocity of one stage is that stage's rise over its own run.

prompt: A body goes 25 m out from O along a straight line, waits, then comes 40 m back along the line. Where does its displacement/time graph end?
options: At −15 m, below the time axis
On the time axis, at 0 m
At 15 m, above the time axis
answer: At −15 m, below the time axis
explain: Coming 40 m back from 25 m carries the body 15 m past O, to $25 - 40 = -15$ m, so the graph ends below the axis. This is step 3 of See it, where the trolley ended at $-15$ m too.

twin.prompt: A body goes 30 m out from O, waits, then comes 42 m back along the same line. Where does its graph end?
options: At −12 m, below the time axis
On the time axis, at 0 m
At 12 m, above the time axis
twin.answer: At −12 m, below the time axis
twin.explain: 42 m back from 30 m ends 12 m past O: $30 - 42 = -12$ m, below the axis.

optionNotes.option: On the time axis, at 0 m
optionNotes.why: Coming back further than it went takes the body past O, below the axis.
42 m is the return leg's length, not where the body ends.

optionNotes.option: At 12 m, above the time axis
